newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia is rich but no money for aid, ADB says.
newsitem.headline: Asia is rich but no money for aid, ADB says.

text.p: The magic of a free market economy has brought untold wealth into Asia, but apparently not enough to dole out to those who have been excluded from the region's economic boom.

Three days of pondering at a hotel in this southern Japanese city drove home that conclusion to Asia's finance ministers on Tuesday as they ended the 30th annual meeting of the Asian Development Bank.
The ADB's dilemma is that despite Asia's riches, almost one billion people, 30 percent of its population, lives in poverty.
ADB president Mitsuo Sato noted that the region's strong economic performance has continued, despite some slowdown in East and Southeast Asia.
Although the bank's primary mission remains the reduction of poverty, it must improve efficiency and adapt to the changes in the world's fastest-growing region, delegates said.
"I think we will lose our relevance unless we change," Sato said at the end of the three-day meeting.
"Unfortunately, private money will not go into areas where the commercial rate of return is low ... which includes areas of social and environmental concern," Sato told the closing news conference.
The bank, owned by 56 countries, is being pushed aside by two factors:
-- Traditional donors have tightened their purse strings as they have begun facing budgetary constraints.
-- The freeing of economies in the region has led to large flows of private capital.
Japan, the biggest donor, warned at the meeting's opening session on Sunday that it could not continue to be as generous with its aid because its own fiscal situation had deteriorated.
Malaysia and Thailand responded to Japan's announcement with moral posturing on how countries could not abdicate responsibility towards the poor.
Both Malaysia and Thailand, until recently recipients of aid, have now turned donors.

"We are concerned with the declining proportion of contribution from the donors' resources and would like to strongly urge traditional donors to share your wealth," Thailand's finance minister Amnuay Viravan told fellow members of the bank.
The ADB has a soft loan window called the Asian Development Fund, which was recently replenished, but many members have said they cannot continue contributing to it.
With no money to hand out, the ADB has to think of other ways of helping in the region's development.
"Some members are suggesting we step up our private sector operations while others think governments should continue to provide aid," Sato said.

The bank set up a private sector group two years ago to fund small greenfield projects and an advisory panel to the bank recommended it be expanded and that the bank market its products in a better way.
Its formation was welcomed by members but some countries hoped the policies would not be affected by richer countries.
"We have been very supportive of the institute but I think in all decisions ... it will have to take the views of member states," Malaysia's deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim told Reuters.
Malaysia has been very critical of donor nations, saying they attached too many conditions to aid.
Sato said the consensus at the meeting was that the ADB did have a future, not as a lender, but as a catalyst and policy adviser.
But some of its poorest members said they hoped their voices will still be heard, even as the bank strives to change with the times.
